archiveRecords.title: The role of depressive symptoms, episodic memory, and executive functioning on prospective memory: New insights from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Over half of self-reported memory mistakes involve prospective memory (PM), forgetting to recall and to perform a future intention. PM performance is important for functioning in daily life and may be influenced by other underlying cognitive abilities or by depressive symptoms. To date, no large-scale studies have delineated the associations between depressive symptoms, episodic memory, and executive functioning on PM in middle-aged and older adults, while controlling for sociodemographic variables.  Data were drawn from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA), a prospective cohort study using a population-based sample. 16,124 adults (age range 45 to 86 years) at baseline and 13,619 adults at follow-up were included. Mixed-effects modelling was used to examine the effect of depressive symptoms and cognitive abilities on event- and time-based PM, while controlling for age, sex, education, wealth, and self-reported social standing.  Lower depressive symptoms and higher executive functioning predicted better PM performance. Interestingly, depressive symptoms interacted with both executive functioning and episodic memory to predict PM, over and above the main effects. Episodic memory was positively associated with event-, but not time-based PM. Discussion Executive functioning, depressive symptoms, and episodic memory predict PM performance. Moreover, higher cognitive functioning is protective against the negative influence of depressive symptoms on event- and time-based PM. Altogether, these findings clarify how both cognitive and emotional factors correlate with the ability to remember to complete practical tasks in daily life.

archiveRecords.title: Discrimination and Depressive Symptoms: The Role of Psychological Resilience across Racial and Ethnic Groups
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: This study aimed to identify distinct typologies of discrimination experiences and their association with depressive symptoms among older adults across racial/ethnic groups and the potential moderating role of psychological resilience across racial/ethnic backgrounds.  Data from 11,832 respondents (65% non-Hispanic White, 18% non-Hispanic Black, 13% Hispanic, and 4% Other) in the 2016/2018 Health and Retirement Study Psychosocial Leave-Behind Questionnaire were analyzed. Six discrimination types (e.g., disrespect, poor service in restaurants, perceived as unintelligent) and a 12-item resilience index covering domains such as perseverance despite major setbacks, adaptability to change, and recognition of inner strengths were assessed.  Latent class analysis identified three distinct typologies of discrimination experiences: (C1) Low discrimination—low across all experiences, (C2) Microaggressions—elevated probabilities of disrespect, poor service at restaurants, and being perceived as unintelligent, and (C3) Pervasive/threatening discrimination—high across all experiences, including being feared and harassed. Regression models showed that for non-Hispanic Whites, both C2 and C3 were associated with higher depressive symptoms; for non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic individuals, only C2 was linked with more depressive symptoms; for the Other category, only C3 was related to more depressive symptoms. Higher resilience was associated with fewer depressive symptoms across all groups but moderated the effects of C2 and C3 for non-Hispanic Whites and only C2 for Hispanic individuals. Discussion Findings highlight discrimination as a mental health risk factor for older Americans and suggest that psychological resilience may mitigate its impact, contingent on experience type and racial/ethnic . Implications for policy and practice are discussed.

archiveRecords.title: Do Changes in Sense of Purpose in Life Predict Charitable Giving Among U.S. Older Adults? The Moderating Role of Financial Planning Horizon
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Demographic shifts associated with population aging are transforming the philanthropic landscape in the United States. Drawing on the life course perspective and socioemotional selectivity theory, this study investigates how psychological and financial planning factors shape prosocial financial behavior in later life. We examine how changes in sense of purpose in life are associated with charitable giving and further evaluate the extent to which this association is moderated by financial planning horizon among U.S. older adults.  Data are from the 2016-2022 waves of the U.S. Health and Retirement Study (N = 5,509). We estimated multivariable logistic regression models including a two-way interaction term, adjusting for prosocial behavior, religiosity, sociodemographic, and health covariates.  Increases in sense of purpose in life during the study period and a long-term financial planning horizon are positively associated with charitable giving in the fully adjusted models. However, our moderation analyses indicate that for older adults with a short-term financial planning horizon, an increased sense of purpose strongly predicts charitable giving, while for those with a long-term financial planning horizon, this association is weaker or negligible. Discussion This study reinforces the value of applying life course and motivational theories to examine prosocial financial behavior and suggests that interventions to increase charitable giving among older adults should consider individual differences in time perspective. This study highlights the potential of targeted interventions that enhance psychological well-being and prosocial financial behavior, taking into account individuals’ motivational framing and structural contexts to support legacy-building.

archiveRecords.title: Global burden and temporal prediction of intestinal obstruction (1990-2021) and the relationship with blood metabolites: an integrated analysis of GBD and Mendelian randomization
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Intestinal obstruction (IO) poses a significant challenge to healthcare systems, particularly in aging societies. This study systematically evaluated the global burden of IO from 1990 to 2021, predicted trends through 2044, and explored potential metabolic risk factors.  Based on the Global Burden of Disease 2021 statistics, we analyzed incidence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) across 204 countries. Trends were quantified using estimated annual percentage changes (EAPC), while frontier and decomposition analyses assessed the impact of population aging. Future trends were projected using age-period-cohort models. Additionally, a two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) analysis was conducted to investigate the relationship between metabolites and IO.  Globally, the age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) showed a slight upward trend, rising from 185.57 to 191.92 per 100 000 between 1990 and 2021 (EAPC: 0.09), whereas the age-standardized mortality rate (ASMR) declined (EAPC: −1.03). Notably, high-SDI regions (eg, the United States, the United Kingdom) exhibited rising DALYs, largely driven by population aging. Projections indicate that by 2044, the ASMR will further decrease to 2.20 (females) and 3.11 (males) per 100 000. The MR analysis identified 13 genetically predicted circulating metabolites associated with IO susceptibility, providing hypothesis-generating metabolic signals that warrant further validation.  While IO mortality has decreased globally, the absolute burden of IO remains substantial in the context of rapid population aging. Future health policies should focus on resource allocation and surgical care for older adults. The identified metabolic signals may provide candidate avenues for future early screening and prevention research in geriatric care.

archiveRecords.title: The contribution of social and economic factors to accelerated biological aging differences between non-Hispanic Black and White adults in the Health and Retirement Study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Biological aging predicts health outcomes beyond chronological age. The relative contribution of social, economic, and health factors to biological aging differences between Black and White adults remains unclear.  In a cross-sectional analysis of 2086 community-dwelling adults aged ≥60 years from the 2016 Health and Retirement Study (1757 non-Hispanic White; 329 non-Hispanic Black), biological age was measured using DNA methylation-based GrimAge. Accelerated aging was defined as having a biological age older than expected for one’s chronological age. We used logistic regression to assess the impact of race on accelerated aging and decomposition analysis to determine factors explaining differences in accelerated aging between Black and White participants. Covariate blocks were: age, education, wealth, social frailty assessed using a composite index measuring social connections, financial autonomy, neighborhood environment, volunteering and employment engagement, behavioral factors (physical activity, alcohol use, sleep disorder, body mass index); medical conditions; and physical disability.  Black participants had higher accelerated aging than White participants (57.1% vs 41.8%; standardized mean difference, 0.3). In the staged decomposition of the biological aging gap, age and education explained 21.1% of the difference. The cumulative explained share rose to 51.8% with wealth, 77.6% with social frailty, 80.3% with health behaviors, 90.5% with medical conditions, and 91.6% with physical disability. In multivariable logistic regression adjusting for all domains, the racial difference was no longer significant.  Social and economic factors largely explained accelerated biological aging differences between non-Hispanic Black and White adults. These findings identify policy-relevant targets to improve healthy aging.

archiveRecords.title: The relationship between parity and late-life frailty: companion dogs as a preclinical model for evaluating factors that aggravate or mitigate the frailty cost of reproduction
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Frailty refers to a state of heightened vulnerability to adverse health outcomes. Animal models of frailty provide an opportunity to probe lifetime events and exposures that drive frailty progression and to evaluate intervention strategies that could mitigate frailty development and its consequences in older adults. The relationship between parity—production of live offspring—and later life frailty in women is poorly understood. Here, we utilize companion dogs to test the hypothesis that production of live offspring comes at a physiological cost, leading to increased late-life frailty. We measured deficit accumulation using a 34-item clinical frailty index in a cohort of 95 geriatric female Rottweilers. The study outcome was late-life robustness, defined as the lowest quintile of frailty in the study population. We found no evidence of reproductive cost. Instead, compared to nulliparous females, parous females were 3× more likely to retain late-life robustness [OR, 95% CI = 3.30,1.16-9.38; p = .025], a relationship not attenuated by adjusting for covariates, including owner-reported reason for nulliparity. Moreover, females with largest number of litters had highest late-life robustness. Finally, employing two measures of early-life health/fitness—earlier-in-life health deficits, lifetime morbidity profiles—could not explain  based on selection. This inquiry introduces a new application of the dog model of frailty for the study of reproduction and deficit accumulation. The linkage we observed between parity and higher late-life robustness is congruent with  of several studies in women, suggesting parous females may have the capacity to dampen the development of later-in-life frailty, which should be further investigated at the genetic and epigenetic level.

archiveRecords.title: Exercise promotes glutamate transporter-mediated glutamate uptake in the striatum to regulate MSN plasticity and alleviate behavioral and functional impairments in PD rats
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: This study investigated whether exercise ameliorates behavioral deficits in a rat model of Parkinson’s disease (PD) by regulating medium spiny neuron (MSN) plasticity via striatal astrocytic excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs). The PD model was induced by 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) and confirmed by apomorphine rotation. Exercised rats underwent 4 weeks of treadmill training. We assessed motor function using beam walking and cylinder tests. Striatal pathology was evaluated via tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunohistochemistry, glutamate (Glu) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, c-Fos tracing, Western blotting for Glutamate-aspartate transporter (GLAST)/ Glu transporter-1 (GLT-1)/N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR), Golgi staining for dendritic spines, and in vivo local field potential (LFP) recording. Compared to controls, PD rats exhibited motor impairment, dopamine depletion, increased striatal Glu levels, NMDAR expression, and β-oscillations, alongside reduced EAAT expression and spine density. Exercise significantly reversed these abnormalities and improved behavior. Notably, pharmacological blockade of EAATs in exercised rats completely abolished these neuroprotective effects, reinstating the PD phenotype. These findings indicate that treadmill exercise upregulates striatal EAATs (GLAST/GLT-1), enhances Glu uptake, reduces extracellular Glu, and suppresses NMDAR overactivation and β-oscillations. This restoration of Glu homeostasis promotes MSN morphological and functional remodeling, serving as a critical mechanism for exercise-induced behavioral improvement in PD.

archiveRecords.title: Adolescent dietary restriction improves cognition and frailty in aged female Wistar rats
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Dietary restriction (DR) is the most studied non-pharmacological intervention for extending both lifespan and healthspan. While previously considered universally beneficial, recent findings indicate that the effects of DR depend on its onset and duration. Although frequently practiced among teenage girls, the effects of DR in this developmental period remain insufficiently investigated, and existing  are scarce. This study aims to determine the short- and long-term effects of mild adolescent DR on the behavior and frailty in aging female Wistar rats. Female Wistar rats were fed ad libitum (AL) or were dietary restricted (70% of AL daily intake) during early adolescence DR (EADR), middle adolescence DR (MADR), or both early and middle adolescence DR (EMADR). Short-term effects were examined using the Open Field (OF) and Y-maze tests, while long-term effects were assessed using OF, Y-maze, and Novel Object Recognition (NOR) tests, along with survival rate and frailty assessments. Long-term effects on cortical synaptic markers were examined by analyzing the expression of synaptophysin (SPH), drebrin, postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD95), and phosphorylated PSD95 (p-PSD95). Despite the absence of early behavioral effects, predominantly beneficial effects on survival, behavior, frailty, followed by changes in synaptic proteins have been noticed at old age. Our  showed onset- and duration-dependent effects of adolescent DR on aged animals. This study is the first to evaluate the lifelong effects of adolescent DR and highlights the importance of early nutritional habits and the need for caution in dietary interventions during critical developmental stages.

archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Polypharmacy is common in older adults with comorbidities. This study aims to estimate its global prevalence, temporal trends, and dose-response associations with adverse health outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) from individual studies were synthesized using random-effects dose-response meta-analysis in studies that provided sufficient quantitative exposure information. A total of 545 studies, providing 565 prevalence estimates, were included, comprising 16 620 414 older adults from 56 countries worldwide. It demonstrated a significant increasing temporal trend in polypharmacy prevalence over calendar years. Compared with non-polypharmacy, polypharmacy was associated with a significantly higher risk of multiple adverse outcomes. archiveRecords.title: Factors associated with mortality in older sepsis patients: a nationwide retrospective cohort study in Germany
archiveRecords.abstract: Sepsis is a leading cause of mortality in older adults, but large unselected cohort data on factors associated with mortality remain limited.  To examine patient characteristics and acute illness features associated with mortality among older patients hospitalised with sepsis in Germany.  We conducted a retrospective, observational cohort study using statutory health insurance data (AOK) of patients aged ≥70 years and hospitalised with sepsis between 2016 and 2019. Outcomes were in-hospital and 90-day post-discharge mortality. Multivariate blockwise logistic regression models were applied to examine associations across conceptual domains.  Of 227 110 older sepsis patients [median age, 81 years (IQR 76–85); 49.2% women], in-hospital mortality was 35.2%. Organ dysfunction, particularly hepatic and renal dysfunction, as well as receipt of organ support including mechanical ventilation and dialysis, showed strong associations with in-hospital mortality. Among 147 080 patients discharged alive, 19.5% died within 90 days. In this post-discharge phase, care dependency and metastatic cancer showed stronger associations with mortality, whereas associations with acute illness features were lower. Female sex was independently associated with lower mortality and conferred a survival advantage after discharge.  The high mortality rate of older sepsis patients is associated with both baseline patient vulnerability and acute illness severity. Care dependency, used as a proxy for functional vulnerability overlapping with frailty, showed a strong association with mortality, particularly after discharge. These findings highlight the importance of integrating preexisting patient vulnerability and acute illness characteristics to guide individualised acute and post-discharge care for older sepsis patients.

archiveRecords.title: Optimizing Hip Key Performance Indicator 1: Time from ED Presentation to Hip Fracture Bed Allocation
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Hip fractures remain a major orthopaedic concern, with mortality approaching 10% at one month and 33% at one year. Hip Pathway Key Performance Indicator (KPI) 1 recommends admission to a dedicated hip bed within four hours of presentation to ED Delays in diagnostics, referral, and bed allocation can significantly impact patient outcomes. This audit has been registered with the Institutional Clinical Governance Quality Improvement Department and is conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines and adherent to all relevant ethical standards.  A mixed-method audit was conducted on all hip fractures presenting to Emergency Department during May 2024, December 2024, August 2025 and January 2026. Data were extracted from Emergency Department records, radiology timestamps, and orthopaedic admission logs to assess timelines for X-ray, orthopaedic referral and bed admission.  A total of 168 hip fracture cases were reviewed (May ’24: 34; December ’24: 54; August ’25: 35; January ’26: 45) Peak presentations occurred outside of standard working hours. The average time to X-ray was 1:30 hours, with referral to orthopaedic averaging 1:52 hours post-imaging. In August 2025 only approximately 40% of patients were admitted to a hip bed within 4 hours, however 76% achieved admission within 8 hours. Delays were primarily due to ED bottlenecks and limited bed availability.  KPI targets are not being consistently met. Structural and procedural inefficiencies hinder timely admission. Recommended interventions include improved staffing and logistics, earlier orthopaedic and ED staff notification, and optimization of the pre-alert system. Ongoing audit cycles will evaluate the effectiveness of these measures post-intervention.

archiveRecords.title: Improving Accuracy of ASA Grading in Patients with Neck of Femur Fractures: A Closed-Loop Audit Incorporating the Clinical Frailty Scale
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Accurate American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status classification is essential for peri-operative risk stratification in patients with neck of femur (NOF) fractures who are typically older, frail, and multimorbid. ASA is a key variable used within the National Hip Fracture Database (NHFD) to adjust for casemix when calculating expected mortality and benchmarking institutional performance. Inaccurate ASA grading may underestimate patient comorbidity and frailty, leading to artificially low expected mortality and misrepresentation of service outcomes. Aim To assess the accuracy of ASA grading in patients admitted with NOF fractures using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), baseline mobility, and comorbidities, and to re-audit performance following targeted quality improvement interventions prompted by concerns regarding NHFD casemix adjustment.  Three audit cycles were undertaken at a UK district general hospital. This  reports Audit Cycle 3, with Audit Cycle 2 as the baseline comparator. ASA grades recorded in the NHFD were compared with revised ASA grades assigned following structured review of electronic patient records, incorporating documented comorbidities, baseline functional status, and CFS. Where CFS was not prospectively documented, frailty was assigned retrospectively from contemporaneous clinical documentation.  In Audit Cycle 2 (n=129), ASA was underestimated in 33 patients (25.6%). In Audit Cycle 3 (n=114), underestimation reduced to 17 patients (14.9%), with no cases of overestimation. The most frequent discrepancy remained revision from ASA 3 to ASA 4. Prospective CFS documentation was absent throughout.  ASA underestimation improved but remains clinically significant. Persistent gaps in frailty documentation risk distortion of NHFD casemix-adjusted mortality. Embedding routine frailty assessment may improve outcome benchmarking.

archiveRecords.title: Hospital at Home—What does the evidence tell us?
archiveRecords.abstract: Hospital at Home (HaH) has emerged internationally as an effective model of healthcare delivery for older adults, providing care within patients’ homes as an alternative to inpatient admission when appropriate. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been rapid expansion of HaH services, of which older people are the majority users. This collection in Age and Ageing journal brings together contemporary evidence examining the evolution, effectiveness, implementation and experience of HaH care for older people. The papers highlight the heterogeneity of HaH models, ranging from admission avoidance and early supported discharge services to comprehensive geriatric assessment-based multidisciplinary care. Collectively, the evidence suggests that well-supported HaH models can achieve outcomes comparable to inpatient care, with evidence supporting cost-effectiveness and reduced care home admission, whilst improving patient experience and increasing time spent living at home. Importantly, the collection also explores the complexities underlying HaH implementation. Several papers demonstrate that successful HaH depends not only on technology, but on multidisciplinary clinical expertise, coordination across services and substantial contributions from informal caregivers. Challenges relating to workforce capacity, digital exclusion, caregiver burden and service integration remain significant.

archiveRecords.title: Early Removal of Indwelling Urinary Catheters is Associated with Reduced Length of Stay and Mortality in Older Adults Undergoing Hip Fracture Surgery
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Indwelling urinary catheters are routinely inserted for older adults admitted with hip fracture with removal recommended on postoperative day one in our local protocol. However, adherence is variable, and there is limited evidence guiding optimal postoperative bladder management in this population.  A retrospective audit of electronic medical records was undertaken for one year of the Australia New Zealand Hip Fracture Registry at a single quaternary centre. Rates of trial removal of indwelling catheters (TROC) on postoperative day one were assessed. Outcomes included catheter reinsertion, bowel management, length of stay (LOS), and 12-month mortality. Multivariable analysis adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, and usual place of residence.  A total of 327 patients were included (median age 84 years; 66.4% female). Most patients were living at home prior to admission (67.9%), with 32.1% from aged care. Overall, 89.9% were deemed suitable for day-one TROC, but only 36.4% underwent catheter removal. Regular laxatives were prescribed in 40.4% and were not associated with successful TROC (p=0.56). Catheter reinsertion for urinary retention occurred in 16.8% (n=18). Mean LOS was significantly shorter in TROC group compared with those without removal (20.1 ± 16.8 vs 24.4 ± 18.5 days; p=0.047). Patients undergoing day-one TROC were more likely to be alive at 12 months (adjusted odds ratio 2.30, 95% CI 1.25-4.26; p=0.003).  Early removal of indwelling urinary catheters following hip fracture surgery is associated with a four-day reduction in length of stay and improved 12-month survival. These findings support active postoperative bladder management and warrant further prospective evaluation, including strategies avoiding routine catheterisation

archiveRecords.title: A Service Evaluation of the Falls Prevention Guidelines for the Older Person in the Emergency Department (ED)
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Falls are a major cause of death and disability worldwide, leading to functional decline and impacting quality of life. This highlights the importance of effective falls assessment and prevention strategies in this cohort. On average 55% of individuals reviewed by the Frailty Interdisciplinary Team (FIT) presented to the ED with a fall. This aim of this study is to evaluate adherence to the falls subjective and  assessments as part of the FIT standardised comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA). Methodology Data was collected from the CGA over a one-month period. This included falls history, dizziness symptoms, lying/standing BP, vestibular screen and balance assessment. Data was recorded on excel by a trained administrator.  57% of individuals presented to ED with a fall. 76% of these had a history of falls and 32% reported dizziness symptoms on questioning. 68% of individuals demonstrated frailty symptoms. 81% of subjective questions were recorded appropriately. 68% of these patients had a lying/ standing BP completed, 29% had a vestibular screen completed and 0% had a balance outcome measure completed. All individuals had a functional mobility assessment in the ED.  The  revealed inconsistent adherence to standardised procedure for falls assessment by FIT in the ED. While it is suggested that the assessment in its totality is onerous in a busy ED environment, further analysis of the barriers to this would be necessary. The CGA, based on these , has been adapted to ensure that core aspects are adhered to more consistently and that non-core aspects are performed on a case-by-case basis.

archiveRecords.title: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) in the Emergency Department (ED) Enables Detection of Cognitively Vulnerable Older Adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Assessment of frailty syndromes allows identification and modification of significant risk factors for ED presentations. Research identifies cognitive impairment as an independent risk factor for injurious or multiple falls in older adults. Scores of 1, 2 or 3 in the 4AT assessment are suggestive of a cognitive vulnerability such as MCI. Studies demonstrate that without further assessment and tailored multi-disciplinary intervention, cognitively vulnerable older patients presenting to ED are up to 50% more likely to re-present for further care with the same acute need. The aim of this research was to identify the prevalence of cognitively vulnerable older adults presenting to ED with falls. Method Over a one-month period, consecutive patients presenting with a fall were assessed by the Frailty Interdisciplinary Team (FIT) using a standardised assessment. Data collected, as part of routine care, was prospectively entered onto Excel by a trained administrator. Age, gender, Clinical Frailty Score (CFS), 4AT score and presence or absence of prior dementia were recorded. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics.  128 patients were assessed during the study period. 7.8% (n=10) of patients ≥75 years, presenting to ED with a fall had a 4AT score of 1 to 3, with no previous dementia diagnosis. Mean age was 84.7 years (4 males, 6 females) and mean 4AT was 1.8.  FIT assessment effectively identified a cognitive vulnerability in a significant number of older adults presenting to ED with a fall. Detection of cognitive vulnerability will prompt a more detailed formal assessment of cognition and individualised interventions to support patients and/or carers, potentially reducing re-presentation to ED.

archiveRecords.title: Frailty Predicts Adverse Outcomes after Emergency General Surgery in Older Adults – A Multicentre Snapshot Audit on Frailty Prevalence in Irish Hospitals
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction As the population ages, older patients with complex comorbidities are increasingly being admitted to hospitals with acute surgical pathology. Understanding the impact of frailty on unscheduled surgical care is needed to guide future service provision. This prospective collaborative study assessed the impact of frailty on outcomes after emergency general surgery.  Audit approval was granted for prospective snapshot study across eight hospitals. For fourteen consecutive days, all emergency general surgery admissions >60 years was screened for frailty using the Clinical Frailty Score. Electronic records were reviewed for demographics, comorbidities and inpatient course at 30 days, and the national death registry for twelve-month mortality. Outcomes between frail and non-frail patients were compared using SPSS.  Across 112 call sessions, 277 patients >60 years were admitted. Mean age was 76.0 years (+/- 8.76) and 52% were frail (n=135/269). Across all admissions, 104 (41.6%) patients required a procedure and 46 (16.7%) required surgery. Similar numbers of frail and non-frail patients underwent surgery under general anaesthesia (14% vs 19.5%, p=0.264), though proportionally more frail patients required ICU care post-op (42% vs 22%). Out of 21 laparotomies, one patient was seen by a geriatrician. Frailty was associated with higher rates of any complication (p  High levels of frailty and frailty-associated morbidity were noted amongst emergency surgical admissions. Significant investment in collaborative pathways between surgeons and geriatricians is required to optimally manage this high-risk cohort.

archiveRecords.title: Recent breakthroughs in blood-based biomarkers of Alzheimer disease: opportunities and challenges in older adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Recent advances in Blood-Based Biomarkers (BBMs) are transforming the diagnostic landscape of Alzheimer Disease (AD), with plasma p-tau217 emerging as a highly accurate and scalable diagnostic marker of AD pathology. Across multiple analytical platforms, plasma p-tau217 has demonstrated consistently strong diagnostic performance for the detection of amyloid pathology. The interpretation of BBMs in older adults presents unique challenges due to the high prevalence of multimorbidity, chronic kidney disease, polypharmacy and frailty. Although these factors may influence absolute biomarker concentrations, current evidence suggests the diagnostic performance of p-tau217 remains largely preserved across diverse older populations when interpreted appropriately. Frailty may modify the relationship between AD pathology and clinical expression of mild cognitive impairment/dementia and may influence the absolute concentration of BBMs underscoring the importance of contextualising test  within a comprehensive assessment. Importantly, these factors should not preclude a clinical-biological diagnosis of AD. The clinical value of BBMs such as p-tau217 in older adults lies not in their use in isolation, but in their integration with a gerontologically attuned diagnostic pathway. Current evidence and international guidelines support the use of BBMs only in symptomatic older adults presenting to specialist services and not in asymptomatic individuals. This commentary reviews recent advances in BBM performance, emerging clinical guidelines, real-world evidence and potential diagnostic pitfalls relevant to older adults. We propose that incorporating BBMs within a Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment framework offers a pragmatic approach to achieving timely, accurate and equitable clinical-biological diagnosis whilst preserving the holistic, person centred principles of geriatric medicine.

archiveRecords.title: Hospital-at-home and beyond: experiences of patients, caregivers and general practitioners with out-of-hospital care for moderate-to-severe lower respiratory tract infections in older adults—a qualitative study
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Hospital-at-home (HaH) may help address rising healthcare demands in ageing populations by providing hospital-level care outside the hospital. In the Netherlands, an integrated care pathway (ICP) ‘The Hague Respiratory Tract Infection Care Bridge’, was developed for adults aged ≥65 years with moderate-to-severe lower respiratory tract infections, offering care through HaH, hospital-at-nursing-home (HaNH) or hospital admission. This study explored experiences with this ICP among the different care settings from the perspectives of patients, informal caregivers and general practitioners (GPs).  Semi-structured interviews were conducted with participants across the 3 pathways, including 34 patients, 33 informal caregivers and 7 HaH GPs. Data were analysed using deductive thematic analysis guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research.  Three themes emerged from patient and informal caregiver interviews: matching care to needs, shared decision-making and communication, and organisational collaboration. HaH and HaNH were generally seen as positive alternatives to hospitalisation, although feasibility depended on patients’ and caregivers’ physical and emotional circumstances. Overall satisfaction with care was high. Two themes were identified from GP interviews: practical feasibility and engagement in the HaH-pathway. Overall, GPs supported out-of-hospital treatments, but faced barriers regarding unclear responsibilities, minimal involvement in triage and fragmented communication across providers.  Delivering hospital-level care outside the hospital for older adults requires context-sensitive, individualised approaches that align with patients’ and informal caregivers’ circumstances. Perceived safety and acceptability depended on this alignment and on effective organisational collaboration. Sustainable integration of HaH in GP practice requires clear communication pathways and greater involvement in decision-making. These findings provide practical guidance for implementing HaH and HaNH in acute care for older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Are there sex differences in the influence of insomnia symptoms and sleep duration on the trajectory of neuromuscular strength decline?
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction A few longitudinal studies investigating the effect of sleep problems on the decline in neuromuscular strength (NMS) have produced conflicting .  To examine sex differences in how insomnia symptoms (IS) and sleep duration (SD) affect the trajectory of NMS decline.  A longitudinal study with an eight-year follow-up period was conducted involving 6429 participants from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) aged 50 or older. Participants with grip strength ≥27 kg for men and ≥16 kg for women were included. IS were investigated using a questionnaire adapted from Jenkins. SD was classified as short (≤6 h), ideal (>6 to  While an increase in IS was linked to a greater NMS decline rate in men (−0.02 kg per year; 95% CI: −0.04 to −0.01), women with SD ≥9 h experienced a higher rate of decline (−0.14 kg per year; 95% CI: −0.26 to −0.03).  Sex differences were observed in the influence of sleep problems on the rate of NMS decline. Insomnia has a greater effect on men, whereas longer SD affects women more.

archiveRecords.title: SipTilSend: Sustainability of a Quality Improvement Initiative to Reduce Pre-operative Fluid Fasting in Orthopaedic Patients – A Re-audit PDSA Cycle
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Orthopaedic patients frequently undergo prolonged pre-operative fasting due to unpredictable emergency theatre scheduling. Excessive fasting contributes to dehydration, delirium and peri-operative complications in this frail population. Guidance recommends fasting for 6 hours for solids and 2 hours for clear fluids. Our unit previously introduced the SipTilSend initiative, permitting clear fluids until transfer to theatre, demonstrating reduced fasting duration. We performed a further PDSA cycle to evaluate sustainability of this practice change.  A closed-loop re-audit was conducted in a tertiary university hospital. Consecutive hip fracture patients undergoing operative management were included. Fluid fasting time was defined as the interval between last documented oral fluid intake and arrival in theatre reception. Following the initial project, interventions were reinforced through staff education, ward prompts and multidisciplinary engagement with nursing, orthogeriatric and anaesthetic teams. Fasting times were re-measured and compared with previous audit cycles. Peri-operative aspiration events were recorded as a safety outcome.  Forty patients were included (mean age 74.1 years; 25 female, 15 male). Mean fluid fasting time was 11.2 hours (median 9.75 hours; range 0–36 hours). Compared with the previous PDSA cycle (average 3h45min), fasting duration increased, indicating reduced adherence to the pathway over time. Several patients were allowed fluids close to theatre transfer, demonstrating partial adoption. No peri-operative aspiration events occurred. One patient developed post-operative hospital-acquired pneumonia without clear association to fluid intake.  Re-audit demonstrates deterioration in compliance with SipTilSend despite prior improvement, highlighting challenges in sustaining quality improvement interventions. Ongoing education, visible prompts and theatre engagement are required to embed practice change. Liberalised clear fluid intake remains safe and should be reinforced as standard peri-operative care for hip fracture patients.

archiveRecords.title: How social, psychological, and spiritual needs are supported in the last months of life: evidence from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing end-of-life interviews
archiveRecords.abstract: End-of-life care includes social, psychological, and spiritual support in addition to medical care. Population-level evidence on whether these non-medical needs are met in the last months of life, who provides such support, and how it is perceived remains limited.  We analysed end-of-life proxy interviews from deceased participants aged 55 years and older in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (n = 507). Outcomes included whether social, psychological, and spiritual needs were met in the last three months of life, and how support was provided and perceived. Analyses included multivariate probit models adjusted for sociodemographic and end-of-life factors. Findings Individuals died at a mean age of 83 years (range 55–105). Social and psychological needs were met for most individuals (81.8% and 77.8%); among those with spiritual needs (n = 227), 74.4% had these needs met. Support was provided predominantly by family members, with limited involvement of formal services, and was generally rated as good or excellent and helpful. Living alone was associated with lower probabilities of having social, psychological, and spiritual needs met, while dementia was associated with lower probabilities of having social and psychological needs met (P  Reliance on informal networks creates inequities in non-medical end-of-life support, particularly for older adults living alone or with dementia, underscoring the need for more integrated public health approaches.

archiveRecords.title: Time to Analgesia- a Geriatric Emergency Medicine Audit in Patients Presenting with Head Injuries
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Older adults are less likely to receive analgesia in the emergency department. Untreated pain is associated with longer stays and increased complications. The Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM) guidelines recommend adequate analgesia administration within 15 minutes of presentation. We performed an audit to assess time to analgesia, implemented recommendations and reaudited noting improvement in administration times. A significant proportion do not receive analgesia begging the question are we adequately assessing and treating pain in this cohort? Methodology: We audited patients ≥75 years presenting to the Emergency Department. Our inclusion criteria was: ‘Head Injury’ documented at triage. This population sample was reviewed on the Emergency Department MAXIMssystems by selecting patients who met both criteria. Each patient’s Emergency Department drug kardex was reviewed. It was noted whether the patient had received analgesia and the time it was administered. This was compared to the registration time for each patient and the difference between the two calculated. We noted that this was significantly longer than the recommended 15 minutes and enacted an education programme for staff to endeavour to improve time to analgesia.  The initial  showed that the average time from registration to analgesia was just under 3 hours, repeated interventions throughout February 2026 show significant improvement in time to analgesia and final  are expected within the next 14 days.  A significant proportion of older patients presenting to the Emergency Department with Head Injury will receive analgesia with an average wait time of 3 hours, our intervention shows encouraging improvement in these times.

archiveRecords.title: A Comparison of Inpatient and Rehabilitation Pathways for Older vs Younger Trauma Patients in an MTC
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Ireland’s Trauma Network was developed in 2023 with the introduction of two major trauma centres (MTC). The network is still developing, especially with regard to rehabilitation pathways. The aim of this study was to quantify the variations in these pathways experienced by younger (under 65) and older (65 and above) trauma patients in a major trauma centre.  Data is routinely collected on all patients seen by the inpatient trauma service (IPTS). This database was used to examine the experiences of patients admitted from July 2024 to January 2026. Microsoft Excel was used for data analysis. Ethical approval was not required. All traumatically injured adult patients (over age 16) seen by the IPTS who spent over 48 hours in hospital were included (N=1063). A subsection of 299 patients had Rehabilitation Complexity Scale Extended (RCSE) scores available and therefore were further analysed.  45% (N=482) were under 65, and 55% (N=580) 65 or older. Median length of stay (LOS) was 9 days, with a slight variation between younger and older groups (7 days vs 10). 77% of the younger group were admitted under a surgical consultant, however the majority of the older group (60%) were admitted under medicine. The majority of younger patients (79%) were discharged home, with only 6% going to rehabilitation, whereas 50% of the older group went home and 28% to rehabilitation There was no difference in average admission RCSE scores (14) between the groups.  Although they have similar complexity scores and LOS, there are variations in the admitting speciality and discharge pathways between younger and older trauma patients.

archiveRecords.title: An Audit of Bone Health Assessment on a Rehab Unit
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Bone health assessment is one of the key performance indicators in the Irish Hip Database. Treatment of osteoporosis after a hip fracture is shown to prevent further fractures but is associated with lower all-cause mortality. To ensure our adherence with bone health assessments, we audited our practice in a 48 bed rehab unit. We also designed a bone health round which ensured that our assessment was clearly documented.  We included any patients on the ward that had presented with a fracture. We assessed if there was documented plan for osteoporosis treatment. We also assessed if they had a vitamin D level and a plan for calcium and vitamin D replacement.  20 patients were identified who warranted an assessment. Of those, 15 were postoperative hip fracture patients, the others consisted of pelvic, vertebral, radiusand knee and ankle fractures. All patients were charted for vitamin D. 13 of these patients had already been given bone protection, 6 had a clearly documented plan for bone protection but it had not been given yet. The causes of delay included vitamin D deficiency, dental issues and drug access form pharmacy. One patient did not have a clearly documented plan for bone protection. The most common drug prescribed was denosumab. Of note, 2 different patients did not have denosumab charted on the regular section of their medication chart, as it had been charted as a one-time dose on a previous medication chart.  Our audit showed good adherence with osteoporosis treatment while highlighting areas for improvement including ensuring prescription clarity for continued treatment.

archiveRecords.title: Delving Deeper into Audit to Co-Design a Digital Solution to Improve “Time to Bed” – Irish Hip Fracture Standard
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction The Irish Hip Fracture Standards (IHFS) comprise seven evidence-based clinical standards audited through the Irish Hip Fracture Database. Collectively, adherence to these standards improves patient outcomes. However, IHFS 1 (“time to bed”) remains a national laggard tariff, with compliance significantly lower than other standards, all of which exceed 75% compliance.  &  A two-month audit in 2025 at a Model 4 Trauma Centre examined compliance with IHFS 1. Fewer than 41% of patients with hip fracture reached a dedicated orthopaedic bed within 4 hours of Emergency Department (ED) arrival, marginally above the national average (36%). Process mapping identified delays predominantly occurring prior to diagnosis (X-ray) and orthopaedic review, with a mean time of 3 hours from arrival to specialist assessment. This left approximately 1 hour to secure a dedicated bed under existing workflows. Stakeholder engagement and cross-disciplinary review of admission and referral processes identified significant duplication between digital and paper documentation. This duplication contributed to referral delays, incomplete paperwork, and inefficiencies impacting IHFS 1 compliance.  This service improvement initiative facilitated shared understanding between ED and Orthopaedics of key process bottlenecks. A co-designed digital admission proforma is now being developed to streamline documentation and automate orthopaedic referral. Following pilot testing, this intervention has potential for wider implementation across trauma centres, supporting improved compliance with IHFS 1 and enhancing early care for hip fracture patients nationally.

archiveRecords.title: Overlapping premorbid frailty, multimorbidity and malnutrition and their associations with poor outcomes in patients with stroke
archiveRecords.abstract: Aim This study aimed to explore the prevalence of these overlapping premorbid geriatric conditions and examine the association between the number of these conditions and the risk of mortality and major cardiovascular events within 1 year after acute stroke.  In this single-centre prospective cohort study, consecutive stroke patients admitted between November 2020 and September 2024 were enrolled. Premorbid frailty was assessed using the 33-item Rockwood Frailty Index. Multimorbidity was defined as the presence of two or more chronic comorbidities other than stroke. Malnutrition was diagnosed according to the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition criteria. Patients were categorised according to the number of overlapping conditions (NOCs), ranging from 0 to 3. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events within 1 year after admission. Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for potential confounders were used to estimate adjusted hazard ratios.  Among 781 patients (mean age 77.9 ± 12.6 years; 390 [49.9%] female), 226 patients (28.9%) were NOC 0, 289 (37.0%) were NOC 1, 161 (20.6%) were NOC 2 and 105 (13.4%) were NOC 3. Compared with NOC 0, the adjusted hazard ratios for the composite outcome were 1.52 (95% CI 0.86–2.68) for NOC 1, 2.64 (95% CI 1.44–4.85) for NOC 2 and 5.20 (95% CI 2.77–9.73) for NOC 3.  One-third of patients with acute stroke had overlapping premorbid geriatric conditions. The NOCs was significantly associated with a composite event in a dose–response manner.

archiveRecords.title: Frailty phenotype transitions and functional improvements during a supervised exercise trial in older people with HIV: results from the HEALTH Trial
archiveRecords.abstract: Frailty and sarcopenia contribute to functional decline in older people with HIV (PWH), yet intervention data remain limited. We evaluated changes in frailty phenotype status, sarcopenia-related outcomes and functional performance during a supervised exercise trial and assessed associations between baseline frailty, study withdrawal and intervention response.  The High-Intensity Exercise to Attenuate Limitations and Train Habits in Older Adults with HIV (HEALTH) study randomised sedentary PWH aged ≥50 years to 16 weeks of supervised high-intensity interval training (HIIT) or continuous moderate exercise (CME), both combined with progressive resistance training. Frailty was assessed using Fried’s phenotype; sarcopenia using current consensus definitions and exploratory HIV-specific cut-points. Functional outcomes included 400-m walk performance and fatigue.  Of 118 participants (median age 58 years; 85% male), 94 completed the intervention. Among completers, pre-frailty/frailty status decreased from 48.9% to 30.9% (P  During this supervised exercise trial, favourable frailty phenotype transitions and functional improvements were observed among older PWH, particularly in participants with baseline pre-frailty/frailty. Low sarcopenia prevalence limited  regarding categorical sarcopenia outcomes. Strategies to improve retention among more vulnerable participants may enhance intervention reach and impact.

archiveRecords.title: Adapting the Preoperative Assessment of Older Patients - the Value of Inter-Disciplinary Working Between Geriatricians and Anaesthetists
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Prior to implementation of a Perioperative care for Older People undergoing Surgery (POPS) service at our hospital, older patients ≥65 years with a clinical frailty scale score (CFS) ≥5 were referred to anaesthetics following nurse pre-assessment. Integrating a POPS pathway into preoperative assessment facilitated direct referral for Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA), with anaesthetic input at a weekly multidisciplinary team meeting. We assessed the workability and cost savings of the new pathway.  Complying with ethical standards, data from patients assessed by a geriatrician in a POPS clinic over a 13-month period were reviewed. Additional anaesthetics assessments (notes reviews and/or clinical consultation) were recorded.  182 patients underwent preoperative assessment by a geriatrician – median CFS 6 (interquartile range 5-6), median age 81 (range 75.5-84), and M:F ratio 1.1. The magnitude of the surgical procedure was major (n=16), intermediate (n=62) or minor (n=104). 82% (n=150) required no anaesthetics input. 13% (n=23) underwent geriatrician review and anaesthetics notes review. 5% (n=9) underwent a clinical consultation with both geriatrics and anaesthetics – 7/9 had an initial anaesthetics consultation and 2/9 were referred by the geriatrician for airway assessment. Avoidance of duplicate anaesthetics appointments in this cohort saved £27,450. There were 30 unnecessary anaesthetic interventions in the pathway.  Preparing frail patients for surgery is a complex process vulnerable to duplication. Most patients in the POPS pathway do not require additional anaesthetics input preoperatively, releasing those appointments for non-frail high-risk individuals. However, it is important to recognise when dual assessment is indicated to optimally prepare patients for surgery.

archiveRecords.title: Shared Decision-Making Documentation in Patients Considering Radical Cystectomy for Bladder Cancer
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Shared decision making (SDM) is a collaborative process in which clinicians and patients work together to make healthcare decisions, integrating clinical evidence with patient values and preferences. Radical cystectomy carries significant perioperative risks, necessitating high-quality SDM. This single centre quality-improvement project aims to evaluate and standardise SDM documentation for patients considering radical cystectomy.  Electronic records of all patients considered for radical cystectomy for bladder cancer over a one-year period were reviewed retrospectively. Data were collected from urology clinic letters evaluating SDM documentation; capacity to consent; content (surgical, medical and functional risks, alternative management, natural history without surgery, and use of numerical risk estimates); format (free-text prose or SDM tool).  Eighty-seven patient records were reviewed, of which 83 were eligible for analysis. The median age was 73-years. SDM discussion was documented in 90.4% (n=75). Assessment of capacity to consent was not recorded in any case. Surgical risks were documented in 71.1% (n=58), with numerical risk estimates in 61.4% (n=51); medical risks were documented in 69.9% (n=58); risk of functional decline was documented in 1.2% (n=1). Alternatives to surgery were documented in 50.6% (n=42), and the natural history of disease in 15.7% (n=13). There was no documentation noting use of a SDM tool.  While SDM discussions are commonly undertaken in this patient cohort, documentation is variable, with key risks and the option of non-operative management frequently under-documented. Using a structured SDM tool, such as BRAN (Benefits, Risks, Alternatives and Do Nothing), would standardise documentation and may improve the quality, transparency and consistency of SDM.

archiveRecords.title: Perioperative Decision-Making in a Multidisciplinary Preoperative Clinic: Associations of Frailty Assessment with Treatment Recommendations and Mortality in a Non-Oncological Cohort
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Frailty is increasingly recognised as a dynamic condition; however, in patients referred for surgery, particularly those with advanced comorbidity, baseline frailty remains a strong marker of short-term prognosis. The role of Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) in perioperative medicine, continues to evolve, particularly in aligning treatment plans with patient priorities and anticipated benefit.  We conducted a retrospective observational study of a cohort of consecutive non-oncological patients referred to a multidisciplinary geriatric perioperative assessment clinic. Baseline frailty was categorised after CGA and by using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). The primary outcome was recommendation of a non-operative /conservative /palliative treatment pathway following CGA and shared decision-making. Secondary outcomes included mortality at 3 months and 1 year. Associations were explored using logistic regression and categorical analyses.  Eighty-nine patients were included. Increasing frailty was strongly associated with a non-operative or palliative pathway (OR 3.70 per one-point increase in CFS, 95% CI 1.90–7.20; p  In a non-oncological perioperative cohort, baseline frailty was strongly associated with both treatment recommendations and mortality. Frailty assessment provided essential prognostic context to support shared decision-making and appropriate perioperative planning. These findings highlight the value of CGA in perioperative medicine.

archiveRecords.title: Fast-Track Arthroplasty in an Older Adult Population: Patient Satisfaction, Recovery Outcomes, and Protocol Adherence
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Total hip and knee arthroplasty are increasingly performed in older adults with multiple co-morbidities and complex peri-operative needs. Fast-track pathways aim to optimise care, maintain function, and improve patient experience in this population. This study evaluated patient satisfaction and functional recovery following elective joint replacement in an older population managed within a fast-track pathway.  A prospective observational study included 107 patients aged 65 years or older undergoing elective hip (n=69) or knee (n=38) arthroplasty. Patients were managed using a standardised fast-track protocol incorporating pre-operative education, multidisciplinary assessment, multimodal analgesia, neuraxial anaesthesia where appropriate, early mobilisation, and functional discharge criteria. Satisfaction, peri-operative experience, mobilisation, and recovery outcomes were assessed during admission and at follow-up. Protocol deviations and peri-operative haemoglobin levels, blood loss, and anaesthetic technique were recorded. The study was conducted in accordance with accepted ethical standards and institutional governance requirements.  Overall protocol compliance was 22%. Satisfaction at five-week follow-up remained high (100% in knee and 94% in hip arthroplasty). Post-operative day one and two pain scores were higher after knee arthroplasty. Higher pre-operative analgesic requirements were associated with increased post-operative pain (mean score 3.3 vs 3.9). Early mobilisation was achieved in most patients, and the majority returned to their pre-operative level of independence.  Fast-track management of elective hip and knee arthroplasty in an older population is associated with high patient satisfaction and favourable functional recovery. Low protocol compliance highlights the need for targeted implementation strategies in peri-operative care for older adults

archiveRecords.title: Pre-Operative Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment for Frail Older Surgical Patients: A Service Model
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Pre-operative Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) prior to surgery is recommended for all patients living with frailty, although no standardised model exists. We describe a model of care at a tertiary surgical centre embedded within an existing pre-operative pathway.  This is a descriptive study of 100 consecutive patients seen in a pre-operative geriatrician-led CGA clinic from March 2023 until November 2024. Referrals to the clinic were made following anaesthetic pre-operative assessment or after discussion at a ‘High-risk Anaesthetic’ multi-disciplinary team meeting. Data was collected from electronic medical records. The study was registered within the organisation as a service evaluation.  Mean age was 79 years; 50% were male. Mean Clinical Frailty Scale score was 5. Mean Charlson Comorbidity Index was 6. Polypharmacy was present in 92%, with de-prescribing in 42%. 27% of patients had cognitive impairment. Surgical specialties included Orthopaedics (33%), Uro-Gynaecology (23%) and Vascular (17%). 50% did not undergo surgery; active shared decision-making was the leading reason (52%), and 1-year mortality was 12%. In the operative group, 40% had a post-operative geriatrician review. 16% developed post-operative delirium. Median length of stay was 7 days. 72% were discharged to their pre-operative level of care. 30-day and 1-year mortality was 2% and 10%, respectively. For both groups, 1-year survivors had lower mean Charlson co-morbidities scores than those who died (5 [range 3-12] versus 7 [range 5-10]; p=0.04).  We describe a service identifying frail patients within an existing pathway who might benefit from surgery. For those who had surgery, the majority went home to preexisting levels of care. Mortality at 1 year was high for all patients.

archiveRecords.title: One-Year Outcomes Following Conservatively Managed Fragility Fractures of the Proximal Humerus: A Retrospective Cohort Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Proximal humerus fractures are the third most common fragility fracture after proximal femur and distal radius fractures. Non-operative management remains the mainstay of treatment, as evidence consistently shows no clear functional superiority of surgical intervention. However, reliable access to structured pathways remains limited for patients with proximal humerus fractures, in contrast to the established standards of care for proximal femur fractures, limiting the optimisation of recovery, function, and secondary prevention of further falls and fracture. This study aimed to evaluate one-year outcomes following conservatively treated proximal humeral fragility fractures in our unit, focusing on readmission, subsequent fracture, and mortality rates.  A retrospective review of all conservatively treated fragility fractures of the proximal humerus over a 2-year period was conducted. Patient demographics as well as all cause readmission, further fragility fracture and mortality within 1 year of fracture were recorded.  A total of 180 patients were included. 135 (75%) were female. Average age was 73 years. All cause 1-year readmission rate was 25% (N=45) while mortality rate was 10% (N=18). 6.1% (N=11) had a further fragility fracture. Older age and male sex were statistically significant risk factors for readmission (p-values of 0.011 and 0.002 respectively).  Older adults with non-operatively managed proximal humeral fractures experience high rates of readmission, re-fracture, and mortality within one year. Early access to Fracture Liaison Services or specialist gerontological care is recommended to optimise recovery and reduce the risk of subsequent falls and fractures.

archiveRecords.title: Stable Pelvic Ring Fractures in Older Patients Attending a Major Trauma Centre Emergency Department
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction There is limited evidence regarding best practice for the treatment of pelvic ring fractures with no national KPI’s such as those for neck of femur fractures. The Frailty Intervention Team (FIT) provides rapid holistic assessment for older patients in the emergency department (ED). FIT reviewed the care received by patients who sustained a pelvic ring fracture with the aim of preventing deconditioning and promoting functional independence.  Over a three-month period FIT reviewed 18 patients with a pelvic ring fracture. Time to admission, pain relief and additional fractures were considered. All data were entered into an excel sheet.  Thirteen patients were admitted with only five admitted within 6 hours of presentation. Of the 18 patients reviewed, 3 were not prescribed analgesia prior to referral for admission. There were 4 different forms of analgesia (Paracetamol, opioids (codeine, oxycodone), NSAIDs (naproxen, ibuprofen, paracoxib, diclofenac) and transdermal lignocaine, prescribed to the other 15 patients by the ED physicians. Once admitted, all patients had changes made to their analgesia regimen. Five of the eighteen patients (28%) sustained an additional fracture other than a pelvic ring fracture.  Only 38 % of this patient group were admitted within six hours which is substantially below the HSE target of 95% for patients over 75. There is no uniform approach to the prescribing of pain relief for this patient group. Over a quarter of these patients sustained an additional fracture highlighting the complexity of this cohort. This patient group may benefit from a more standardised approach to pain relief to enable earlier mobilisation and assessment.

archiveRecords.title: What Matters Most to Older Adults Attending a Major Trauma Centre Emergency Department (ED) after a Fall
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Directing care goals according to what matters most to patients is one of the four elements of an Institute for Health Improvement Age-friendly hospital system. The intention is to shift the power to the patient by directing providers towards addressing what the person values most. Patients are routinely asked ‘What matters to you’ (WMTY) by an ED based Frailty Interdisciplinary Team (FIT). The aim of this study is to thematically analyse WMTY for older adult patients presenting to ED after a fall as assessed by FIT, over a 3-month period.  Routinely collected data from a CGA was entered prospectively onto excel by a trained administrator. Gender, CFS score, diagnosis and WMTY was recorded. An analysis of WMTY was separated into themes for the older person presenting to ED after a fall.  273 falls patient were seen. Mean (SD) CFS was 5 (1.2). The female to male ratio was 1.7:1. 216 (79%) patients had documentation of WMTY. Five themes emerged. 1. Health and independence 32% (n=70) 2. Home 27% (n=59). 3. Family and friends 21% (n=45) 4. Personal concerns i.e. happiness and religion 11% (n=23) 5. Hobbies 9% (n=19).  Recorded WMTY in this frail older population centred around health and independence, home and family/friends. Individual personal concerns were important when expressed. Further improved compliance on asking patients WMTY could lead to greater improvements in individualised care. Next steps are to educate the team on the importance of asking older adults WMTY to help direct compassionate care for these patients and also align interventions towards meaningful patient-centred goals.

archiveRecords.title: Cost-effectiveness of comprehensive geriatric assessment: systematic review of economic evaluations
archiveRecords.abstract: Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) can be resource-intensive as its delivery involves multidisciplinary personnel, multidimensional assessment, care planning and follow-up. The aim of this systematic review is to appraise and synthesise evidence on the cost-effectiveness of CGA across settings.  Full economic evaluation studies examining CGA were searched across five databases. We included studies involving adults aged ≥65 years who were identified as living with frailty or at risk of adverse outcomes. Two independent reviewers screened studies against eligibility criteria and extracted data using a pretested extraction form. Reporting quality was assessed using the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards framework. We reported the  through narrative summaries, tables and figures.  A total of 4864 studies were identified, of which 17 were included across 7 settings (11 community, 6 hospital). Of 13 cost-utility analysis studies, incremental quality-adjusted life years ranged from −0.06 to 0.54 and incremental costs ranged from €−12 744 to €29 785. The probability CGA was cost-effective ranged from 0% to 98.9% across stated willingness-to-pay thresholds (cost-effective in 5/13, not cost-effective in 7/13, 50% chance in 1/13). Two studies showed that cost-effectiveness can vary by frailty severity and residential status. The resource intensity of CGA varied, ranging from 25% (case management protocol) to 81% (comprehensive assessment). Only five studies accounted for informal caregiver costs. The reporting quality ranged from 38% to 90%.  The cost-effectiveness of CGA remains uncertain. Variations in resource intensity of CGA, frailty severity, residential status of older adults and setting may explain this heterogeneity. PROSPERO registration no CRD42023492586.

archiveRecords.title: Navigating Care after Spinal Trauma- An Older Adult’s Journey from Hospital Admission to Home
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Falls from standing height are a leading cause of major trauma in older adults, accounting for approximately 61% of injuries, with half occurring in the home environment. This active 81 year old lady sustained a C5 spinal fracture that required surgical fixation following a low energy fall and resulted in a prolonged and complex hospital admission with life altering consequences, including dysphagia.  A retrospective patient journey mapping approach was used to explore the lived experience of an older adult following traumatic cervical injury. The journey was traced from admission to a major trauma centre through prolonged acute care and inpatient rehabilitation to eventual discharge home with community services. The mapping focused on patient experience, individual rehabilitation needs, interdisciplinary team working and transitions of care through rehabilitative services.  This case documents a 260 day hospital admission and highlights the significant complexity involved in delivering individualized inpatient rehabilitation for older adults with traumatic injuries. This lady required substantial medical, nursing, dietetics, speech and language therapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychology input as she recovered from multiple neurosurgical fixations and an intensive care stay including ventilation and various complications. Coordination of care and communication across multiple specialities was paramount to navigating difficult decisions like enteral feeding in planning for discharge home.  This patient journey illustrates the substantial personal and system level challenges associated with traumatic injury in older adults. The findings emphasize the importance of coordinated interdisciplinary care, flexible rehabilitation pathways, and a patient centred approach to support recovery and discharge home.

archiveRecords.title: Prevalence of sarcopenia and individual- and country-level risk factors in 36 countries: pooled analysis of nationally representative individual data
archiveRecords.abstract: Sarcopenia is an age-related condition that contributes to disability and healthcare burden worldwide. Yet cross-national evidence on prevalence and multi-level risk factors is limited.  We pooled data from 10 nationally representative or population-based ageing studies, including 144 226 adults aged ≥50 years from 36 high- and middle-income countries. Sarcopenia and severe sarcopenia were defined using 2019 revised European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People criteria. Prevalence was standardised by age and gender within each country. We examined associations between sarcopenia and individual-level sociodemographic and health characteristics, and country-level socioeconomic indicators.  Sarcopenia prevalence ranged from 2.1% to 17.4% across 36 countries, with 16 countries above 5.0% and three above 10.0%. Approximately 92.7 million of 1.07 billion adults ≥50 in these countries were projected to have sarcopenia. At the individual-level, higher risk was associated with older age, gender (men), lower education, being unmarried or not partnered, non-full-time employment, lower household wealth, current smoking, non-recent drinking, physical inactivity and ≥2 chronic diseases (e.g. men: RR = 1.47; 95% CI: 1.32, 1.64). At the country-level, higher gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, higher Gender Development Index and lower Labor Force Participation Rate were associated with lower sarcopenia risk (e.g. GDP per capita: RR = 0.42; 95% CI: 0.30, 0.60).  Sarcopenia varies widely across countries and is more common in middle-income than high-income settings, pointing to a pattern shaped by both personal and contextual conditions. Addressing the emerging burden of sarcopenia will require integrated strategies targeting modifiable risk factors while tackling contextual and structural inequalities.

archiveRecords.title: Iatrogenic Chlordiazepoxide Toxicity in an Older Adult
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Chlordiazepoxide is a long-acting benzodiazepine used in the treatment of alcohol withdrawal syndrome and has been associated with prolonged sedation and respiratory depression long after last administration of the drug.  A 70 year old female with a history of excessive alcohol use, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and falls presented following a fall resulting in a neck of femur fracture. Chlordiazepoxide was pre-emptively started on a fixed dose schedule with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment Alcohol Scale Revised (CIWA-Ar) score of 5 and subsequently weaned according to symptoms as per protocol. Four days post-operatively she became drowsy, unresponsive and desaturated. Initial assessment considered respiratory sepsis with respiratory failure.  Despite her last dose being 27 hours prior, experience with chlordiazepoxide accumulation prompted a stat dose of flumazenil 0.2mg with instantaneous though temporary improvement in mental status. A further 2 doses resulted in immediate reversal of sedation and hypoxia. A continuous infusion was commenced once transferred to Intensive Care Unit. The flumazenil infusion was required for 8 days before successful discontinuation.  The patient received a cumulative dose of 470 milligrams over 76.5 hours. Chlordiazepoxide has a half-life of 5 to 30 hours, with active metabolites with half-lives of up to 200 hours, in some case reports still being detectable at one month. Delirium is common in hospitalized older adults and symptom triggered approach to benzodiazepine dosing, designed to reduce the cumulative dose, can still result in large doses being received. Latency between last dose and prolonged sedation may obscure the causative connection. Consideration should be given to use of shorter acting drugs in this cohort.

archiveRecords.title: Developing a National Digital Hub to Support Scale-Up of Perioperative Medicine for Older People (POPS) Services
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Despite clear evidence supporting POPS services in cost-effectively improving outcomes, NHS implementation remains variable. This reflects challenges in mobilising knowledge into local practice. Knowledge mobilisation (KM) offers a structured way to bridge this evidence–practice gap. This project describes development of a national POPS resource toolkit on NHS Futures, designed as a KM platform supporting organisations to establish sustainable POPS services, translating evidence into practice.  The platform was developed using the NHS Knowledge Mobilisation Toolkit, emphasising the Knowledge-to-Action (K2A) framework and KM maturity model. Clinicians and patient and public involvement contributors co-produced and curated resources. Content was organised to support service implementation by linking POPS evidence to clear , target audiences, and practical routes to action. Resources were structured across three domains: clinical, service development, and education/training. The toolkit supports an online network with a community of practice, facilitating peer learning, contextual adaptation of resources, and bidirectional knowledge exchange. Evaluation was embedded from inception via iterative reflection cycles using the KM maturity model, refinement of K2A approaches, and Futures analytics to assess reach and engagement.  The POPS toolkit employs KM by translating evidence and experiential knowledge into accessible, actionable tools. Early engagement data show substantial reach, with 5,697 Workspace views since platform establishment (4 months). Feedback indicates increased confidence in service development, reduced duplication of work, and stronger connections between emerging and established POPS teams. The community of practice supports shared problem-solving and dissemination of tacit knowledge not routinely captured in formal guidance.  Embedding POPS resources within a structured KM framework enables scalable, adaptive, and sustainable implementation of POPS services.

archiveRecords.title: Revision Joint Surgery in Orthopaedic Trauma Theatres: An Increasingly Complex Problem?
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction As rates of primary hip and knee arthroplasty rise alongside an aging population, a corresponding increase in revision joint surgery is inevitable. Indications include prosthetic joint infection, periprosthetic fracture/dislocation and mechanical failure of implant components. These procedures are technically complex with a risk of perioperative complications such as major blood loss. This study aimed to evaluate annual theatre resource utilisation for revision surgery at a major trauma centre and its evolution over time, and to characterise the complexity of this patient population.  A retrospective service evaluation was conducted of revision arthroplasty and periprosthetic fracture procedures performed in two orthopaedic trauma theatres 2019-2025. Data were extracted from electronic patient records and theatre management system.  A total of 584 procedures were included. The annual number increased 227% from 52 in 2019 to 127 in 2025. Median anaesthetic time was 90 minutes (IQR 55-210) and surgical time 125 minutes (IQR 90-165). Patients had a median age of 75 (IQR 67-83) with 52% male. Median length of stay was 17 days (IQR 10-39). In-hospital mortality was 3.2% and 45% were discharged to a nursing home or other hospital. Discharge documentation was incomplete in 114 cases; of the remaining 470 patients, 87% had at least one documented co-morbidity, including cardiac (22.7%), respiratory (10.2%), renal disease (3%), and dementia/stroke (6.6%).  Revision joint surgery and associated perioperative care represents an increasing and resource-intensive proportion of the emergency orthopaedic workload. Patients are older, increasingly frail and with significant co-morbidities. The associated perioperative morbidity is reflected by prolonged hospital stay, discharge to nursing home and other care facilities and in-hospital mortality.
