reviewRecords.title: Collaborative Development of Perioperative Care for Older People in Wales: From Regional Partnership to National Planned Care Funding
reviewRecords.abstract: Introduction Older patients undergoing planned surgery benefit from Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) via a Perioperative care for Older People undergoing Surgery (POPS) service. This cost-saving intervention that improves perioperative outcomes is only available in two of six Welsh health boards who provide surgical services. We describe how collaboration between local clinicians and national groups facilitates standardisation of perioperative care for older people in Wales.  A cross-health-board collaboration was established between two POPS services, supported by the Bevan Commission – a Welsh health and social care think tank. Through an ‘Adopt and Spread’ programme we developed an implementation toolkit to share learning and guide service models, workforce planning and outcome frameworks. This conformed to ethical standards. It was complemented by collaboration with NHS Wales Performance and Improvement funding to provide staff secondments and start-up costs in each health board for up to twelve months.  All 6 health boards expressed an interest in developing or expanding a POPS service. Four health boards (67%) have utilised the support and funding thus far - 2 to start new services and 2 to accommodate a new surgical specialty. Limitations to uptake included capacity of geriatricians to support the service and hesitation due to a non-substantive funding model.  Regional collaboration can gain national traction and act as a catalyst for service development. This model provided implementation support and resources to accelerate POPS service mobilisation in new sites and an existing service expansion - an important step towards reducing unwarranted variation in perioperative pathways for older surgical patients in Wales.

reviewRecords.title: Multidisciplinary recommendations for palliative and supportive care in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and related disorders
reviewRecords.abstract: Prion diseases, of which Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is the most common, are fatal neurodegenerative disorders and are often rapidly progressive. They are associated with a significant palliative care burden for patients and families, ranging from prognostic uncertainty to complex symptom management to caregiver distress. Healthcare professionals face unique pressures when caring for these patients, which can include a lack of familiarity with this rare diagnosis and rapidly evolving symptom needs due to accelerated clinical deterioration. We convened a multidisciplinary panel of experts from around the UK, including palliative care doctors, general practitioners, physician and nurse specialists in prion diseases, and a lived experience representative to compile practical, consensus-based recommendations for managing prion diseases, much of which can also be applied to other rapidly progressive dementias. In this article, we examine the available evidence base for managing various aspects of prion diseases. Where evidence is limited, we suggest best practices informed by decades of our collective experiences.

reviewRecords.title: Falling into ICU: Outcomes and Resource Utilisation of Patients Admitted to ICU Following Neck of Femur Fracture Surgery
reviewRecords.abstract: Introduction Neck of femur (NOF) fractures confer a high mortality risk for older patients with an incidence of over 4000 people per year in Ireland. The high comorbidity burden in patients with NOF requires combined perioperative management involving orthopaedics and geriatric medicine. Postoperative management pathways vary between institutions and in hospitals without dedicated high-dependency postoperative care beds, intensive care unit (ICU) admission may be used to facilitate enhanced monitoring for high-risk patients. Understanding the organ support requirements of NOF patients admitted to ICU may help inform postoperative pathways and resource utilisation.​  A retrospective chart review, not requiring institutional ethical approval of all NOF admissions to ICU between November 2024 and December 2025 with outcomes assessed at 3 months and 6 months post admission (N=31).  Over half patients required no organ support. Three patients needed ventilatory and vasopressor support, and two required ventilatory support alone. Patients who required no critical care supports had a median ICU length of stay of 4.95 days (IQR 3.4-6.3 days). Patients who required organ support had a median ICU length of stay of 8.6 days (IQR 4.1-10.5 days).  Over half of the patients admitted to ICU required no organ support during their ICU stay. HDU level care or earlier step-down from ICU may be appropriate where available, reducing pressure on higher level critical care resources. This audit was not designed to capture admission indication which limits interpretation regarding the appropriateness of ICU admission, however it could inform policies regarding ICU utilisation and inform postoperative pathways following NOF fixation surgery.

reviewRecords.title: FIT for Home Post Trauma
reviewRecords.abstract: Introduction Frailty Intervention teams (FIT) successfully working within emergency departments (ED) improve outcomes for frail older adults through facilitating reduced patient experience time, identifying frailty symptoms, and supporting early discharge. A comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) is completed by the members of the team ensuring all the patients’ needs are considered when creating a tailored care plan. To improve discharge efficiency, a model-four hospital’s FIT analysed the barriers to discharging frail older patients presenting after a fall. FIT reviews approximately 200 frail older adults a month with 50% of these presenting after a fall.  Over a four-week period 48 patients referred to FIT for assessment were reviewed. Patient outcomes and barriers to discharge were logged in Excel then analysed to identify recurring themes and opportunities for service improvement.  Of the 48 patients reviewed 33 (69%) were discharged after assessment of the FIT. Three patients had acute medical needs and were not suitable for discharge (New Afib, delirium 4AT: 12, laceration requiring plastics review). Three common themes emerged from the remaining 12 patients who were not discharged. Four patients experienced pain that was not well controlled, five had a change functional mobility that could not be supported on discharge e.g. assistance of two. Three patients did not have support to assist with personal activities of daily living (PDL) e.g. toileting  Uncontrolled pain, change in mobility status and insufficient social support to facilitate PDL’s were the common barriers to facilitating discharge. There is potential to improve patients experience through educating emergency doctors about the teams’ findings. Future collaboration between FIT and emergency medicine is required to devise a common pain ladder for frail older adults.

reviewRecords.title: Costs and cost-effectiveness of palliative care in residential aged care homes: a scoping review
reviewRecords.abstract: Palliative care is increasingly recognised as a core component of healthcare delivery in residential aged care (RAC) homes, yet its economic implications remain unclear. Understanding costs and cost-effectiveness is essential for guiding resource allocation decisions in these settings.  To map the evidence on the costs and cost-effectiveness of palliative care delivered in RAC homes, and to identify gaps in the evidence base.  A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews checklist. Searches were conducted in the PubMed, SCOPUS, Embase, CINAHL and CENTRAL databases. Studies reporting on quantitative economic outcomes of palliative care in RAC settings were included. Findings were summarised using narrative synthesis.  Of the 3182 items identified, 15 studies were included. Three categories of economic outcomes were identified: care delivery costs (n = 3), healthcare system costs (n = 10) and cost-effectiveness outcomes (n = 2). Studies examining care delivery costs reported additional costs associated with palliative care. Among studies assessing healthcare system costs, six reported reduced costs, one reported increased costs and three reported mixed findings varying by time horizon and care continuity. Two full economic evaluations reported favourable cost-effectiveness findings compared with usual care, although the statistical significance of findings varied.  Economic evidence on palliative care in RAC remains limited and methodologically heterogeneous, constraining robust  regarding its economic value. Future research should prioritise rigorous economic evaluations that comprehensively capture healthcare and social care costs while incorporating patient-centred outcomes to better assess the value of palliative care in RAC homes.

reviewRecords.title: NOFs Lead to Coughs: A Proactive Post-Operative Dysphagia Management Pathway for Hip Fracture Patients
reviewRecords.abstract: Introduction Neck of femur (NOF) fractures are high-risk injuries in older adults, frequently complicated by frailty and post-operative delirium. Evidence suggests 34% of NOF patients are dysphagic within 72 hours of admission (Smithard 2007). Aspiration pneumonia occurs in up to 15% of cases and triples 30-day mortality (Neuman 2014). Current referral models are often reactive; this project developed a dedicated "NOFs Lead to Coughs" clinical are pathway, specifically targeting the post-operative phase.  The pathway was designed using a "Referral-Assessment-Management" framework. Inclusion criteria were defined as patient’s ≥65 following surgical repair of a fragility hip fracture. The referral trigger was shifted from symptomatic coughing to a proactive mechanism based on post-operative cognitive status. Patients with a post-operative 4AT score ≥4, indicating likely delirium and associated swallowing vulnerability, are referred to Speech and Language Therapy (SLT) for screening.  The resulting pathway prioritises three pillars: Referral: Automatic SLT screening triggered by pre or post-operative delirium (4AT ≥4) or persistent sedation following anaesthesia. Assessment: Clinical evaluation of alertness, postural stability, and airway protection, specifically addressing the fluctuating swallow safety seen during the post-operative window. Management: Implementation of evidence-based dysphagia management, which may include texture modifications and compensatory swallowing strategies. The pathway emphasises MDT coordination to ensure safe hydration and nutrition are maintained throughout the post-operative recovery.  Implementing a structured post-operative SLT pathway addresses a critical gap in delivery of comprehensive care for this patient cohort. By standardising screening based on post-operative delirium status (4AT), we can proactively mitigate aspiration pneumonia risk and improve clinical outcomes for this frail surgical population.

reviewRecords.title: Reporting race and ethnicity in aging in place research: A systematic review
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Despite differences in housing experience across people from different racial and ethnic groups in the United States, race and ethnicity are not frequently emphasized in aging in place literature. This review cataloged the approach to race and ethnicity (active or passive) taken by quantitative aging in place research articles. This review also tested whether structural research elements were associated with the approach taken. Research Design and  This study included original research articles with samples of noninstitutionalized older U.S. residents. Included articles addressed an aspect of aging in place related to the physical home, used statistical modeling, and were published between 2014 and 2023. Because an initial database search in this interdisciplinary field did not produce a comprehensive list of articles, the review sample was constructed through manual review of journal tables of contents.  Approximately one third (35.16%) of the 91 sample articles took an active approach to race and ethnicity. The regression model did not detect statistically significant associations between structural research elements and active approaches; however, wide confidence intervals indicate that meaningful effects cannot be ruled out.  Even in the presence of a strong and historic association between race and ethnicity and housing, a passive approach to race and ethnicity was most common. This presents a gap in the existing body of aging in place literature. Practical suggestions for addressing this gap through future research are presented. A multidisciplinary symposium to develop more formal suggestions is recommended.

reviewRecords.title: Effect of Social Support on Psychological Well-Being Among Older Adults in Low- and Middle-Income Countries of the Asian Region: A Systematic Review
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: To summarize and compare the literature on social support and its effect on psychological well-being among older adults in low- and middle-income countries of the Asian region. Design A Systematic review. The review was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews with identification number XXXXXXXXXX. Data Sources Retrieved data from PubMed, CINAHL (EBSCO), PsycINFO, Scopus, and Cochrane Centre Register of Controlled Trials databases. The literature review was conducted from 2018 to 2024. Review  The review complies with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis guidelines.  Initially, 4,615 records were identified using the predefined search strategy. Out of 95 articles selected for full-text screening, 27 met the inclusion criteria. This review identified family and friends as the primary source of social support, enhancing their overall well-being. The higher levels of social support, whether emotional, informational, companionship, or tangible, improve older adults’ psychological well-being and quality of life, including reduced depression, anxiety, and loneliness.  The emotional and mental health of older adults can be diminished significantly due to the lack of adequate social support, leading to a cascade of adverse outcomes. This challenge is especially prevalent in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where older adults often struggle to access formal healthcare, social services, and a structured community support system. Promoting robust social networks is crucial for older adults’ well-being and sustainable aging strategies in low-resource settings.
